Elham is a young, unmarried author who was working on the second or third book in an ongoing series when she Fell — that is, she crossed over during sleep, both body and mind transporting into the very realm she believed she had only been imagining. The notes are clear that this crossing is specific to the sleeping state and cannot occur any other way. Once there, she understood that what she had taken for creative inspiration was something closer to vision: her stories were not invention but a record of real, ongoing events in another dimension, and she is not the first Author to have written of this realm, only the most recent. Humans do not naturally reside here, and the realm's higher-ups maintain a registration system so that any new Author's arrival is flagged almost immediately — a system framed in the notes as not always sinister in intent, but still one that strips privacy entirely. Elham therefore has to conceal that she is both human and an Author, because exposure on either count puts her at risk. Her situation is further complicated by the fact that even the hero of her own books may have grounds to be unsettled by her, given how intimately Authors tend to write about the people whose lives they document.

The most pressing danger at present is that the draft places her early in the story inside the domain of the principal antagonist — a figure whose name the notes plan to weave around the words "Silver" and "Heart," and who is described as something closer to a far-reaching, Capricorn-of-Inkheart style force than a conventional mafia boss. He is not without a soul, and a softer side of him once existed or may still exist — but that is precisely what makes Elham's position so precarious: she knows this through her writing, not through any trust he extended to her, and he would have every reason to view that knowledge as a threat or a tool. His right hand, known as the Sparrow, is the reason she winds up in that domain: the Sparrow brought her there under the premise of taking her somewhere she could get something she needed, but Elham knows exactly who he is and who he serves, making acceptance of his offer its own kind of danger; refusal risked arousing suspicion from him or, worse, his leader. He operates nearby and earns loyalty through pragmatic, if coercive, recruitment rather than outright force. Elham cannot leave too quickly without arousing that same suspicion, and her notes acknowledge she cannot be certain how much of her unease is genuine threat and how much is paranoia — but the notes also make plain that the moment she slips, someone in that domain could unmask her entirely.
